newsitem.title: USA: Northeast dairy plan likely to fall, US judge says.
newsitem.headline: Northeast dairy plan likely to fall, US judge says.

text.p: U.S. District Judge Paul Friedman, while refusing to issue a preliminary injunction, has said there was "substantial" likelihood the Northeast Dairy Compact was created improperly.
The compact empowers a commission representing the six New England states to adjust the price of milk bound for grocery stores. It can raise prices by up to 25 percent, if desired.
Milk Industry Foundation, which filed suit to overturn the compact, said Friday it was "encouraged by the judge's statement that we may well prevail in the end."
Arguments in the case were set for February 25.

In a ruling late Thursday, U.S. Judge Paul Friedman rejected the foundation's request for a preliminary injunction. He said the MIF was "unlikely to succeed" with an argument Congress unconstitionally delegated its powers in letting Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman decide whether to implement the plan.

However, Friedman said, "it has a substantial -- indeed, almost a certain -- likelihood of success" with its argument that Glickman failed to adequately justify, under a federal paperwork law, the need for the compact.
New England lawmakers Friedman's ruling would allow the commission running the compact to hold hearings next week.
"The court has narrowed the issues and has moved this process closer to a solution which we hope will allow the compact to do its work," Vermont's congressional delegation said in a statement.
New Englanders say the compact will help dairy farmers stay in business in a densely populated region with high costs.
Critics say the compact is a cartel that effectively keeps out lower-priced milk from other parts of the nation. It also is contrary to efforts to deregulate dairying, they say.
Under the 1996 farm policy law, the compact would be limited to a three-year life.
